sentences.text: Teratornis merriami stood approximately 75 cm tall with an estimated wingspan of 3.5 to 3.8 meters and a weight between 12.5 and 15.0 kg.
The anatomy of its wings included fused finger bones with a specialized shelf on the index finger that helped support long primary feathers for utilizing strong upcurrents in flight.
Teratornis had fused toe bones like modern birds, but part of the index toe formed a platform that increased its wing loading.
Its legs were similar to those of an Andean condor but more robust, and its claws could have been used to tear pieces from prey.
Teratornis merriami was the largest flying bird encountered by humans in its lifetime.
The species was large enough and possibly aggressive enough to attempt feeding on human infants, though not regularly.
More than 100 fossil and subfossil individuals of Teratornis have been found across California, Oregon, Nevada, Arizona, and Florida, with the majority coming from the La Brea Tar Pits.
The species Teratornis woodburnensis was discovered in 1999 at Legion Park in Woodburn, Oregon, north of the La Brea Tar Pits.
The partial skeleton of Teratornis woodburnensis indicates an estimated wingspan of over 4 meters.
Teratornis likely primarily inhabited cliff terrain to facilitate takeoff and soaring flight.
Analysis of skull morphology suggests Teratornis merriami was an active predator capable of swallowing prey whole, rather than just a scavenger.
Teratornis merriami likely swallowed small prey like frogs and lizards whole and fed on carrion similarly to condors or vultures.
Teratornis could maintain flight in changing air currents due to emarginated primary feathers that separate and move independently.
Teratornis merriami likely swallowed small prey the size of rabbits in one bite and consumed carrion similarly to vultures and condors.
Analyses of its skull and beak suggest that fish were an important part of its diet.
It is very possible that Teratornis hunted aquatic prey in a manner similar to fish eagles.
Teratornis merriami lived similarly to modern condors, but its larger beak suggests it was a more active predator.
The genus Teratornis was described by L. H. Miller in 1909.
Teratornis belongs to the extinct family Teratornithidae.
The type species of the genus Teratornis is Teratornis merriami.
The genus Aiolornis was formerly known as Teratornis incredibilis but is now considered distinct enough to be its own genus.
All known Teratornis remains date to the Late Pleistocene, except for one partial Early Pleistocene skeleton found in Florida.
The genus Teratornis lived from the Calabrian to the Holocene, spanning 1.8 to 0 million years ago.
It is debated whether the memory of Teratornis persisted enough to form the basis of thunderbird myths.
